claims.text: Carbothermal shock synthesis can overcome structural or chemical instability during catalytic operation at 773–1173 K.
The starting materials are crystalline, near-equiatomic, single-solid-solution nanoparticles containing at least five metals.
The relevant catalytic operating-temperature range is 773–1173 K.
Carbothermal shock can rapidly fabricate high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Carbothermal shock fabrication of high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles can occur within seconds.
Carbothermal shock maintains precise control over elemental distribution in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Carbothermal shock maintains precise control over nanoparticle stoichiometry.
A high-entropy effect mediates operational stability.
Severe lattice distortion mediates operational stability.
Sluggish diffusion kinetics mediate operational stability.
A cocktail effect mediates operational stability.
Control of elemental distribution and stoichiometry through carbothermal shock could produce a stable, single-phase solid solution.
The resulting single-phase solid solution would have high mixing entropy.
Carbothermal-shock-synthesized nanoparticles will have greater structural stability than nanoparticles made without carbothermal shock.
Carbothermal-shock-synthesized nanoparticles will have greater chemical stability than nanoparticles made without carbothermal shock.
Thermally exposed carbothermal-shock-synthesized nanoparticles will be compared with control nanoparticles made without that intervention.
X-ray diffraction, electron microscopy, energy-dispersive spectroscopy, and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy will measure structural and chemical changes.
The hypothesis is falsified if the treated nanoparticles show similar or worse stability and catalytic performance than the controls.

contradictions.description: The initial state is already specified as crystalline solid-solution nanoparticles, whereas carbothermal shock is described as the method that fabricates those nanoparticles. The hypothesis does not explain how a synthesis method is applied as an intervention to nanoparticles that already exist.
